oneliner.t: First-term Democratic congresswoman from Phoenix and former Phoenix vice mayor, elected in 2024 with 70.9% after winning a three-way primary by about 40 votes; unopposed in the July 21, 2026 primary (37,553 votes), she faces No Labels nominee Alan Aversa, Green nominee David Redkey and write-ins in a district rated Solid/Safe D.

born.note: Birthplace in both; exact date from Wikipedia only.

hometown.t: Scottsdale, Arizona (raised there; Chaparral High School)

upbringing.t: Born in Seattle to parents who emigrated from Iran after the 1979 revolution, she grew up in Scottsdale and attended Chaparral High School. As a high-school student she organized for Barack Obama's 2008 campaign and tutored Somali refugees with her mother. She earned a bachelor's in international relations at Stanford and a master's at the University of Cambridge as a Gates Cambridge Scholar, then worked on the climate team in UN Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon's office during the Paris Agreement negotiations and later advised Secretary-General António Guterres. She moved back to Arizona and won a Phoenix City Council seat in a March 2021 runoff.

profile.office_years_note: Phoenix City Council Apr 2021–Mar 2024 (about 3 years) plus U.S. House since Jan 2025.

education.school: University of Cambridge (St John's College), Gates Cambridge Scholar
education.note: Ballotpedia lists 2015; Wikipedia says she began the program in 2016. Sources conflict on the year.

career.role: Advisor / senior policy advisor, climate team, Executive Office of the UN Secretary-General (Ban Ki-moon)
Deputy policy director, Global Climate Action Summit (Office of Gov. Jerry Brown)
Senior policy advisor to Secretary-General António Guterres
Phoenix City Council, District 7 (vice mayor in 2023)
U.S. Representative, AZ-03 (Natural Resources; Oversight and Government Reform)

platform.t: Campaign site says she has worked to rein in ICE and protect immigrant communities; Wikipedia reports she called for abolishing ICE in January 2026 and traveled to El Salvador in April 2025 over the Kilmar Abrego Garcia case.
Runs on defending reproductive freedom; introduced the 'HER Agenda' on reproductive-health conditions and reproductive leave (per campaign site).
Opposed U.S. military action against Iran in 2025 and condemned the 2026 Iran war; in April 2026 announced plans to file impeachment articles against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

Shifted from a 2024 pledge of military aid 'without additional conditions' to co-sponsoring the Block the Bombs Act (2026) and saying in 2026 that she believes Israel committed genocide in Gaza and Lebanon; says she supports Israeli security and a Palestinian state.

Built her Phoenix record on climate policy (heat-response office, bus electrification) and housing/homelessness spending; 2024 themes also included LGBTQ+ equality, labor and union rights, an 'economy for all' and campaign-finance reform.
Uses her Oversight seat to press for accountability in the Epstein case; voted for the Epstein Files Transparency Act (Nov 18, 2025).
Did not respond to the invitation for the Aug 25, 2026 CD3 debate; has not completed Ballotpedia's 2026 survey.

promises.t: Will 'never put big funders ahead of working families' (campaign-site pledge).
Said in 2026 she will reject financial help from AIPAC and DMFI.

record.t: Wikipedia: 'the youngest female member of Congress.'
Wikipedia: elected Democratic freshman class president in November 2024.

claims.claim: International relations degree from Stanford; master's from Cambridge.

record.t: Wikipedia and Ballotpedia list both degrees. 'With honors' was not checked. The Cambridge year differs between sources (2015 vs. a 2016 start).

claims.claim: In 2014 became an advisor in UN Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon's office and served on the climate team that helped deliver the Paris Agreement.

record.t: Wikipedia: senior policy advisor in Ban's office via the John Gardner Fellowship, spending a year on the Paris Agreement. The 2014 start date is from her own page only.

claims.claim: Deputy policy director for the Global Climate Action Summit (Gov. Jerry Brown's office).

record.t: Not mentioned in the Wikipedia or Ballotpedia material reviewed; Wikipedia says only that she helped plan climate summits.

claims.claim: Youngest woman ever elected to the Phoenix City Council.

record.t: Wikipedia says she was the youngest person elected to the council at the time (a broader claim that includes hers).

claims.claim: Served as Councilwoman and Vice Mayor.

record.t: Wikipedia cites 2023 coverage naming her vice mayor; council service Apr 19, 2021 to Mar 28, 2024.

claims.claim: After Dobbs, passed a resolution making state abortion-law enforcement the Phoenix Police Department's lowest priority.

record.t: Not covered in the Wikipedia material reviewed; no council record opened.

claims.claim: Pushed for more than $140 million for shelter beds, supportive housing and behavioral-health services.

record.t: Wikipedia says she was the first Iranian American elected to public office in Arizona; it does not address the congressional claim.

claims.claim: Ranking Member of the Energy & Mineral Resources Subcommittee.

record.t: Wikipedia lists Natural Resources and Oversight; it does not list subcommittee roles. Committee roster not opened.

claims.claim: Brought over $17 million in federal funding to Arizona in her first year.

record.t: No appropriations or community-project record opened.

claims.claim: Traveled to El Salvador to push for due process for Kilmar Abrego Garcia.

record.t: Wikipedia: traveled to El Salvador in April 2025 to look into his case.

claims.claim: Has opposed Trump's military action against Iran.

record.t: Wikipedia: opposed U.S. military intervention in Iran (June 2025) and condemned the 2026 war (April 2026).

claims.claim: Led the effort to pass Phoenix's Climate Action Plan.

record.t: Wikipedia cites a Climate Action Plan article but does not describe her role; it credits her with creating the Office of Heat Response and Mitigation.

said.t: 2024 position paper: continued U.S. military aid to Israel without additional conditions.

did.t: Co-sponsored the Block the Bombs Act, which would restrict offensive-weapons transfers to Israel; she said her shift reflects changed conditions since 2024.

said.t: Said Israel has the responsibility of investigating allegations of wrongdoing (in the ICC context).

did.t: Voted Yea on H.R. 23 to sanction the International Criminal Court, one of a minority of Democrats.

said.t: Campaign site says she has pressed for accountability and justice for survivors in the Epstein case.

did.t: Voted Aye on the Epstein Files Transparency Act (427–1).

promises_prev.promise: Support continued U.S. military aid to Israel without additional conditions.

evidence.t: 2024 position paper pledge (Jewish Insider); in 2026 she co-sponsored the Block the Bombs Act restricting arms transfers to Israel.

complicating.t: She frames the change as a response to events since 2024 and says she still supports Israeli security. The bill has not passed (status not checked).

evidence.t: Campaign site says she introduced the HER Agenda bills on reproductive health and leave.

complicating.t: Introduced as a minority-party member; no record of floor action found in sources reviewed. Status label reflects introduction without enactment, not a documented block.

entries.t: Pledged unconditional military aid; DMFI endorsed her and spent for her in the primary.
Opposed Sen. Sanders's resolutions to block about $20B in arms sales to Israel.
Co-sponsor of the Block the Bombs Act; an early backer of Rep. Tlaib's Lebanon war-powers resolution; said she believes Israel committed genocide in Gaza and Lebanon.
Position paper called stopping an Iranian nuclear weapon essential.
Supported the (defunct) nuclear deal and opposed U.S. military intervention.
Condemned the 2026 Iran war and called for its immediate end.

aipac_endorse.t: Not endorsed — Track AIPAC shows no AIPAC endorsement label (data 7/5/26). Jewish Insider reports she sought AIPAC's endorsement in 2024 and AIPAC held off, and that in 2026 she said she would reject AIPAC and DMFI help.

Said Sanders's resolution would deny Israel materials needed for deterrence and defense.

In a Zeteo interview said, for the first time, she believes Israel committed genocide in Gaza and Lebanon, citing a UN report; condemned the Oct 7 attack; supports Israeli security and a Palestinian state; said she would reject AIPAC and DMFI money.
Said she declined an AIPAC-led trip to Israel in 2025, citing her opposition to war with Iran.

lobby.t: Track AIPAC lists $1,161,274 in career pro-Israel money: $1,156,274 in independent expenditures (DMFI named, 2024 primary) and $5,000 in donations. Jewish Insider reported DMFI's 2024 spending for her as 'nearly $300,000' (Aug 2024) and 'more than $400,000' (Jul 2026); the gap with Track AIPAC's figure has not been reconciled against FEC independent-expenditure filings, so treat the $1.16M as unconfirmed. She said in 2026 she will refuse AIPAC and DMFI support.

note.t: Calendar-2025 annual (signed Aug 13, 2026): Schwab Value Advantage money fund $1M–$5M (dividends $100,001–$1M), a Phoenix condo in a revocable trust ($500K–$1M), a second Phoenix condo via Pena Blanca LLC ($250K–$500K; rent $15K–$50K), a Roth IRA ($100K–$250K) and a Phoenix pension.
